Subject: Post-call recap: performance targets & concurrency requirements

Thanks Jorge & Priya — great conversation today. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we have alignment on SLO/throughput expectations and how Redwood can meet them. Notes below taken while on the call: 

- Business SLOs: 95th percentile response time <= 150ms for short prompts (<=256 tokens) for the assistant feature; occasional longer-generation streams ok for conversation histories.
- Throughput target: steady-state ~200 requests/sec across US region during business hours (peak observed ~300 req/s for 10–15 minute bursts).
- Concurrency: application expects up to 40 concurrent in-flight requests from the product (these are independent user requests, not streaming chunks). We also want connection pooling support from the SDK to keep TCP / TLS handshakes low.
- Streaming: for multi-turn assistant flows we need token-level streaming to UI (low-latency first-byte + steady token delivery). Priority is first-byte latency for perceived snappiness.
- Availability & fallbacks: want canary fallback to a cheaper model for brief capacity bursts and an error budget for degraded quality.

Open questions we agreed to follow up on:
1) How Redwood enforces hosted API rate limits (per-key vs per-tenant) and how that maps to the 40 concurrent requirement.
2) Burst behavior / token-bucket characteristics and whether temporary bursts will be throttled or queued.
3) If Dedicated or Reserved capacity is required to guarantee the 95p 150ms SLO at 300 req/s bursts.

Next steps I suggested on the call:
- Dylan (SE) to confirm concurrency model + recommended connection pooling settings and provide a short runbook.
- I'll send a draft mutual action plan with the SLOs and a proposed Dedicated capacity quote if needed. (attached: acme-mapping-sla.xlsx)
- Schedule a technical deep-dive next week with your infra team to size dedicated capacity or discuss host-level rate-limit increases.

Thanks — I’ll follow up with specific numbers from Dylan and a short proposal.

Hi Jorge / Priya — thanks for the follow-up. Wanted to lay out how Redwood approaches concurrency & rate limits and give concrete recommendations tied to your numbers. Long-ish but tried to be explicit.

1) Concurrency model (hosted API):
- We track two related limits: concurrent in-flight request slots and sustained requests/sec (RPS). Concurrent slots are used for active inference work (GPU/CPU). RPS protects routing and overall cluster capacity.
- Default hosted keys: 50 concurrent in-flight requests and 600 RPS per API key in the US region. These defaults are tuned for general usage but can be raised for qualifying customers.
- For streaming requests, a streaming session consumes a concurrent slot for the duration of the stream. If you have many long-running streams, that counts more towards concurrency than short single-shot requests.

2) Mapping your requirements to Redwood: 
- You indicated steady-state ~200 RPS with peaks up to 300 RPS and 40 concurrent in-flight requests. The hosted default (50 concurrent / 600 RPS) would technically allow this traffic, but it depends on model size, average token generation time, and whether streams hold slots for many seconds.
- If your streams are short (first-byte under 100ms and average stream duration < 1s) hosted should be fine with a modest rate-limit raise and our connection pooling best practices.
- If you see long-lived streams (several seconds to tens of seconds) for many concurrent users, those will consume concurrency slots and risk throttling during peaks.

3) Connection pooling & SDK guidance:
- Use persistent HTTP/2 or keep-alive TLS connections from the frontend. We recommend 8–12 concurrent connections per app server with multiplexing (HTTP/2) — the Redwood SDKs support HTTP/2 and connection reuse.
- Client-side retry/backoff: implement small jittered exponential backoff for 429s and prefer queueing at the app layer for best-effort requests.

4) Negotiation & options to guarantee SLOs:
- Short-term: we can temporarily raise your hosted key rate limits (concurrency and RPS) for the evaluation period while we monitor token usage and latency. This is a standard approval for customers with predictable traffic patterns.
- Mid-term / production SLOs: we recommend Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) for binding SLAs at 95p ≤ 150ms under your burst profile. Dedicated gives you reserved concurrency pools and predictable tail latency.
- Cost note: rough sizing suggests a Dedicated pool for your US traffic based on model complexity (we estimated N GPU cards) — I'll follow up with a short capacity sketch and a quote.

5) Action items I can take this week:
- Provide a short runbook with exact SDK connection-pooling settings and example client configs.
- Spin up a temporary hosted rate-limit bump for your key for the next 14 days so you can validate under load.
- Draft a Dedicated sizing note and preliminary quote (will include expected concurrency pools and expected 95p latency based on our benchmarks). Attached: redwood-slo-proposal.pdf

Let me know which time slots next week work for the technical deep-dive (I included a couple below).

Thanks,
